content.text:
Good question, and the daily-update part is exactly why this matters for your decision.

The short version: yes, when your data changes frequently, RAG is the default choice, and that's not really controversial. The reason is structural — RAG keeps the knowledge outside the model, in a retrievable store. To reflect today's update, you just re-index or add the new documents. Nothing about the model changes.

Fine-tuning does the opposite: it bakes knowledge into the weights. To update it, you retrain (or run another tuning pass), which is slow and costly relative to just updating an index. For data that changes daily, that's a losing game.

So the "how often data changes" axis has a pretty clear lean: high churn → RAG.

On your second question — "other new approaches" — let me check what's current rather than answer from memory, since this space moves fast.

content.text:
The search confirms the consensus: for data that changes often, RAG is the standard, and the framing across sources is consistent — "how often your data changes" (data volatility) is treated as one of the primary deciding variables, and high volatility points to RAG.

On the "other new approaches" part, a couple of things worth knowing, but with a caveat about scope:

The main "new" thing isn't a replacement for RAG — it's the hybrid pattern. You use RAG for the fresh, changing knowledge (your daily updates), and optionally fine-tune only for how the model behaves — tone, format, following instructions. Notice those are two different jobs: keeping facts current vs. shaping behavior. The freshness axis alone doesn't tell you whether you need the second part.

One caveat I'd flag: even with RAG, "updates daily" isn't fully free. You still have to keep the index in sync — re-embedding changed documents, handling deletions, avoiding stale chunks. That's real data-engineering work, just far cheaper and faster than retraining. So RAG solves the freshness problem but moves the effort into your ingestion pipeline.
